Are Scientific And Religious Explanations Incompatible?

No they are entirely compatible, for now at least.

What injected into our early universe the massive amount of dark energy needed to sustain expansion? Could have been a god, no doubt it was something else but we haven't got any sort of evidence that it wasn't yet.

Why did the infinitely small point that universe began as suddenly and explosively expand? Could have been a god of some description decided to make a universe, or it could have simply been a natural mechanics inherent to such dense points, we have no idea yet.

Is there an edge to the universe? Is it fixed or is it fractal or is it infinite? What is beyond the thin layer of existence we inhabit? Is it nothing but void where normal laws don't apply or is it merely a different larger universe? Could it be such a place could be a heaven or a hell to us? We have no idea there either, no doubt in the future as more and more data is collected and experiments get enough of a ground work to make assessments but for now we don't even know if that's the right question for whatever answer we get.

When the universe first expanded it was made up of near enough half matter and half antimatter, almost all of which annihilated casting photons around the early universe. We've accounted for a lot of these photons but little over half are unexplainable gone. Where did all this energy go? Was it captured by some god and harnessed? Or simply destroyed to create the universe we know now without interference?

I'm not a religious man but you can find many unknown places to say "God had a plan there and it made us what we are today." through science. I merely listed the physics points that would make sense, no doubt there are many, many more.

This would be less convincing if you didn't leave out all the previous 'good of the gaps' points. What about an earth centered universe? What of disease being caused by sin (roundabout way of saying God)? Religion always fills in the gaps of knowledge with God, but rarely and only incidentally demonstrates an equal contribution to knowledge.

Not that I think science is free from belief in any sense of the word, if you take a good look at scientists and their history it is full of beliefs held by its practitioners.

Without furthering the polarized issue on this subject, if one thinks back to when writing first appeared all the way until Christianity become the State religion of the Roman Empire, religion mostly kept to themselves and science mostly kept to themselves. They usually crossed paths for trade, exchanging of ideas, and developing civilizations. Once both became part of a governmental or State mandate (whether for better or for worse,) then polarization started to happen. Please correct me if I am wrong. Thanks!
